{{short description|Point found separated from another, given a point pair}}
[[Image:pappusharmonic.svg|thumb|right|300px|{{mvar|D}} is the harmonic conjugate of {{mvar|C}} with respect to {{mvar|A}} and {{mvar|B}}.<br>{{mvar|A, D, B, C}} form a harmonic range.<br>{{mvar|KLMN}} is a [[complete quadrangle]] generating it.]]

In [[projective geometry]], the '''harmonic conjugate point''' of a point on the [[real projective line]] with respect to two other points is defined by the following construction:
:Given three collinear points {{mvar|A, B, C}}, let {{mvar|L}} be a point not lying on their join and let any line through {{mvar|C}} meet {{mvar|LA, LB}} at {{mvar|M, N}} respectively. If {{mvar|AN}} and {{mvar|BM}} meet at {{mvar|K}}, and {{mvar|LK}} meets {{mvar|AB}} at {{mvar|D}}, then {{mvar|D}} is called the '''harmonic conjugate''' of {{mvar|C}} with respect to {{mvar|A}} and {{mvar|B}}.<ref>R. L. Goodstein & E. J. F. Primrose (1953) ''Axiomatic Projective Geometry'', University College Leicester (publisher). This text follows [[synthetic geometry]]. Harmonic construction on page 11</ref>

The point {{mvar|D}} does not depend on what point {{mvar|L}} is taken initially, nor upon what line through {{mvar|C}} is used to find {{mvar|M}} and {{mvar|N}}. This fact follows from [[Desargues theorem]].

In real projective geometry, harmonic conjugacy can also be defined in terms of the [[cross-ratio]] as&nbsp;{{math|1=(''A'', ''B''; ''C'', ''D'') = −1}}.

==Cross-ratio criterion==
The four points are sometimes called a [[projective range|harmonic range]] (on the real projective line) as it is found that {{mvar|D}} always divides the segment {{overline|{{mvar|AB}}}} ''internally'' in the same proportion as {{mvar|C}} divides {{overline|{{mvar|AB}}}} ''externally''. That is:

<math display=block>\overline{AC}:\overline{BC} = \overline{AD}:\overline{DB} \, .</math>

If these segments are now endowed with the ordinary metric interpretation of [[real numbers]] they will be ''signed'' and form a double proportion known as the [[cross ratio]] (sometimes ''double ratio'')

:<math>(A,B;C,D) = \frac{\overline{AC}}{\overline{AD}} \left/ \frac{\overline{BC}}{-\overline{DB}} \right. , </math>

for which a harmonic range is characterized by a value of &minus;1. We therefore write:

:<math>(A,B;C,D) = \frac{\overline{AC}}{\overline{AD}} \times \frac{\overline{BD}}{\overline{BC}} = -1 .</math>

The value of a cross ratio in general [[Cross-ratio#Six_cross-ratios|is not unique]], as it depends on the order of selection of segments (and there are six such selections possible). But for a harmonic range in particular there are just three values of cross ratio: {{math|{&minus;1, 1/2, 2},}} since &minus;1 is self-inverse – so exchanging the last two points merely reciprocates each of these values but produces no new value, and is known classically as the '''harmonic cross-ratio'''.

In terms of a double ratio, given points {{mvar|a, b}} on an affine line, the '''division ratio'''<ref>[[Dirk Struik]] (1953) ''Lectures on Analytic and Projective Geometry'', page 7</ref> of a point {{mvar|x}} is 
<math display=block>t(x) = \frac {x - a} {x - b} .</math>
Note that when {{math|''a'' < ''x'' < ''b''}}, then {{math|''t''(''x'')}} is negative, and that it is positive outside of the interval.
The cross-ratio <math>(c,d;a,b) = \tfrac{t(c)}{t(d)}</math> is a ratio of division ratios, or a double ratio. Setting the double ratio to minus one means that when {{math|1=''t''(''c'') + ''t''(''d'') = 0}}, then {{mvar|c}} and {{mvar|d}} are harmonic conjugates with respect to {{mvar|a}} and {{mvar|b}}. So the division ratio criterion is that they be [[additive inverse]]s.

Harmonic division of a [[line segment]] is a special case of [[Apollonian circles|Apollonius' definition of the circle]].

In some school studies the configuration of a harmonic range is called ''harmonic division''.

==Of midpoint==
[[Image:Real projective line.svg|right|thumb|150px|Midpoint and infinity are harmonic conjugates.]]

When {{mvar|x}} is the [[midpoint]] of the segment from {{mvar|a}} to {{mvar|b}}, then 
<math display=block>t(x) = \frac{x-a}{x-b} = -1.</math>
By the cross-ratio criterion, the harmonic conjugate of {{mvar|x}} will be {{mvar|y}} when {{math|1=''t''(''y'') = 1}}. But there is no finite solution for {{mvar|y}} on the line through {{mvar|a}} and {{mvar|b}}. Nevertheless,
<math display=block>\lim_{y \to \infty} t(y) = 1,</math>
thus motivating inclusion of a [[point at infinity]] in the projective line. This point at infinity serves as the harmonic conjugate of the midpoint {{mvar|x}}.

==From complete quadrangle==
Another approach to the harmonic conjugate is through the concept of a [[complete quadrangle]] such as {{mvar|KLMN}} in the above diagram. Based on four points, the complete quadrangle has pairs of opposite sides and diagonals. In the expression of harmonic conjugates by [[H. S. M. Coxeter]], the diagonals are considered a pair of opposite sides:
:{{mvar|D}} is the harmonic conjugate of {{mvar|C}} with respect to {{mvar|A}} and {{mvar|B}}, which means that there is a quadrangle {{mvar|IJKL}} such that one pair of opposite sides intersect at {{mvar|A}}, and a second pair at {{mvar|B}}, while the third pair meet {{mvar|AB}} at {{mvar|C}} and {{mvar|D}}.<ref>H. S. M. Coxeter (1942) ''Non-Euclidean Geometry'', page 29, [[University of Toronto Press]]</ref>

It was [[Karl von Staudt]] that first used the harmonic conjugate as the basis for projective geometry independent of metric considerations:
:...Staudt succeeded in freeing projective geometry from elementary geometry. In his {{lang|de|Geometrie der Lage}}, Staudt introduced a harmonic quadruple of elements independently of the concept of the cross ratio following a purely projective route, using a complete quadrangle or quadrilateral.<ref>B.L. Laptev & B.A. Rozenfel'd (1996) ''Mathematics of the 19th Century: Geometry'', page 41, [[Birkhäuser Verlag]] {{isbn|3-7643-5048-2}}</ref>

[[File:Fano parallelogramm.svg|thumb|right|alt=parallelogram with diagonals|{{math|1=''P''{{sub|1}} = ''A''}}, {{math|1=''P''{{sub|2}} = ''S''}}, {{math|1=''P''{{sub|3}} = ''B''}}, {{math|1=''P''{{sub|4}} = ''Q''}}, {{math|1=''D'' = ''M''}}<br>(ignore green M).]]
To see the complete quadrangle applied to obtaining the midpoint, consider the following passage from J. W. Young:
:If two arbitrary lines {{mvar|AQ, AS}} are drawn through {{mvar|A}} and lines {{mvar|BS, BQ}} are drawn through {{mvar|B}} parallel to {{mvar|AQ, AS}} respectively, the lines {{mvar|AQ, SB}} meet, by definition, in a point {{mvar|R}} at infinity, while {{mvar|AS, QB}} meet by definition in a point {{mvar|P}} at infinity. The complete quadrilateral {{mvar|PQRS}} then has two diagonal points at {{mvar|A}} and {{mvar|B}}, while the remaining pair of opposite sides pass through {{mvar|M}} and the point at infinity on {{mvar|AB}}. The point {{mvar|M}} is then by construction the harmonic conjugate of the point at infinity on {{mvar|AB}} with respect to {{mvar|A}} and {{mvar|B}}. On the other hand, that {{mvar|M}} is the midpoint of the segment {{mvar|{{overline|AB}}}} follows from the familiar proposition that the diagonals of a [[parallelogram]] ({{mvar|PQRS}}) bisect each other.<ref>[[John Wesley Young]] (1930) ''Projective Geometry'',  page 85, [[Mathematical Association of America]], Chicago: [[Open Court Publishing]]</ref>

===Maclaurin and Newton identities===
Given two points <math>A</math> and <math>B</math>, let <math>M</math> be their midpoint; we can [[without loss of generality]] give them affixes <math>-1</math>, <math>1</math> and <math>0</math> in the [[complex plane]] respectively. Then, for any point <math>C</math> with affix <math>z</math>, it turns out the harmonic conjugate of <math>C</math> has affix <math>1/z</math>. Calling this harmonic conjugate <math>D</math> yields the following identities:
* Maclaurin: <math>MC \cdot MD = MA^2 = MB^2</math> (which in complex numbers simply becomes <math>z \cdot \frac{1}{z} = 1^2 = (-1)^2</math>)
* Newton: <math>DB \cdot DA = DC \cdot DM</math> (which in complex numbers states that <math>(z + 1)(z - 1) = (z - 0)(z - \frac{1}{z})</math>)

===Quaternary relations===
Four ordered points on a [[projective range]] are  called '''harmonic points'''  when there is a [[tetrastigm]] in the plane such  that  the  first and third are codots and the other two  points are on the connectors of the third codot.<ref name=GBH>[[G. B. Halsted]]  (1906) ''Synthetic Projective Geometry'', pages 15 & 16</ref>

If {{mvar|p}} is a point not on a straight with harmonic points, the joins of {{mvar|p}} with the points are '''harmonic straights'''. Similarly, if the axis of a [[pencil (mathematics)|pencil of planes]] is [[skew lines|skew]] to a straight with harmonic  points, the planes on the points are '''harmonic planes'''.<ref name=GBH/>

A set of four in such a relation has been called a '''harmonic quadruple'''.<ref>[[Luis Santaló]] (1966) ''Geometría proyectiva'', page 166, Editorial Universitaria de Buenos Aires</ref>

==Projective conics==
A conic in the projective plane is a curve {{mvar|C}} that has the following property:
If {{mvar|P}} is a point not on {{mvar|C}}, and if a variable line through {{mvar|P}} meets {{mvar|C}} at points {{mvar|A}} and {{mvar|B}}, then the variable harmonic conjugate of {{mvar|P}} with respect to {{mvar|A}} and {{mvar|B}} traces out a line. The point {{mvar|P}} is called the '''pole''' of that line of harmonic conjugates, and this line is called the '''polar line''' of {{mvar|P}} with respect to the conic. See the article [[Pole and polar]] for more details.

===Inversive geometry===
{{main|Inversive geometry}}
In the case where the conic is a circle, on the extended diameters of the circle, harmonic conjugates with respect to the circle are [[inversive geometry#Inversion in a circle|inverses in a circle]]. This fact follows from one of Smogorzhevsky's theorems:<ref>A.S. Smogorzhevsky (1982) ''Lobachevskian Geometry'', [[Mir Publishers]], Moscow</ref>
:If circles {{mvar|k}} and {{mvar|q}} are mutually orthogonal, then a straight line passing through the center of {{mvar|k}} and intersecting {{mvar|q}}, does so at points symmetrical with respect to&nbsp;{{mvar|k}}.
That is, if the line is an extended diameter of {{mvar|k}}, then the intersections with {{mvar|q}} are harmonic conjugates.

===Conics and Joachimthal's equation===
Consider as the curve <math>C</math> an ellipse given by the equation

:<math>\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} =1.</math>

Let <math>P(x_0,y_0)</math> be a point outside the ellipse and <math>L</math> a straight line from <math>P</math> which meets the ellipse at points <math>A</math> and <math>B</math>. Let <math>A</math> have coordinates <math>(\xi,\eta)</math>. Next take a point <math>Q(x,y)</math> on <math>L</math> and inside the ellipse which is such that <math>A</math> divides the line segment <math>PQ</math> in the ratio <math>1</math> to <math>\lambda</math>, i.e. 
:<math> PA=\sqrt{(x_0-\xi)^2+(y_0-\eta)^2}=1, \;\;\; AQ=\sqrt{(x-\xi)^2+(y-\eta)^2}= \lambda</math>.
Instead of solving these equations for <math>\xi</math> and <math>\eta</math> 
it is easier to verify by substitution that the following expressions are the solutions, i.e.
:<math>(\xi,\eta)=\bigg(\frac{\lambda x+x_0}{\lambda +1}, \frac{\lambda y+y_0}{\lambda +1}\bigg).</math> 
Since the point <math>A</math> lies on the ellipse <math>C</math>, one has
:<math>\frac{1}{a^2}\bigg(\frac{\lambda x+x_0}{\lambda +1}\bigg)^2 + \frac{1}{b^2}\bigg(\frac{\lambda y+y_0}{\lambda +1}\bigg)^2 = 1,</math>
or
:<math>\lambda^2\bigg(\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}-1\bigg) + 2\lambda\bigg(\frac{xx_0}{a^2}+\frac{yy_0}{b^2}-1\bigg) + \bigg(\frac{x_0^2}{a^2}+\frac{y_0^2}{b^2}-1\bigg)=0.</math>
This equation  - which is a quadratic in <math>\lambda</math> - is called ''Joachimthal's equation''. 
Its two roots <math>\lambda_1,\lambda_2</math>, determine the positions of <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> in relation to <math>P</math> and <math>Q</math>.  
Let us associate <math>\lambda_1</math> with <math>A</math> and <math>\lambda_2</math> with <math>B</math>.  Then the various line segments are given by
:<math>QA=\frac{1}{\lambda_1+1}(x-x_0, y-y_0), \;\; PA=\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_1+1}(x_0-x, y_0-y)</math>
and
:<math>QB=\frac{1}{\lambda_2+1}(x-x_0, y-y_0), \;\;  PB=\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_2+1}(x_0-x, y_0-y).</math>
It follows that
:<math>\frac{PB}{PA}\frac{QA}{QB}=\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1}.</math>
When this expression is <math>-1</math> , we have
:<math>\frac{QA}{PA}=-\frac{QB}{PB}.</math>
Thus <math>A</math> divides <math>PQ</math> ``internally´´ in the same proportion as <math>B</math> 
divides <math>PQ</math> ``externally´´.
The expression 
:<math>\frac{PB}{PA}\frac{QA}{QB}</math>
with value <math>-1</math> (which makes it self-inverse) is known as the ''harmonic cross ratio''. With <math>\lambda_2/\lambda_1=-1</math> as above, one has <math>\lambda_1+\lambda_2=0</math> and hence the coefficient of <math>\lambda</math> in Joachimthal's equation vanishes, i.e.
:<math>\frac{xx_0}{a^2}+\frac{yy_0}{b^2}-1=0.</math>
This is the equation of a straight line called the polar (line) of point (pole) <math>P(x_0,y_0)</math>. One can show that this polar of <math>P</math> is the chord of contact of the tangents to the ellipse from <math>P</math>. If we put <math>P</math> on the ellipse (<math>\lambda_1=0, \lambda_2=0</math>)
the equation is that of the tangent at <math>P</math>. One can also sho that the directrix of the ellipse is the polar of the focus.

==Galois tetrads==
In [[Galois geometry]] over a [[Galois field]] {{math|GF(''q'')}} a line has {{math|''q'' + 1}} points, where {{math|1=∞ = (1,0)}}. In this line four points form a harmonic tetrad when two harmonically separate the others. The condition
:<math>(c, d; a, b) = -1, \ \text{ equivalently } \ \ 2 (c d + a b) = (c + d) (a + b),</math>
characterizes harmonic tetrads. Attention to these tetrads led [[Jean Dieudonné]] to his delineation of some [[accidental isomorphism]]s of the [[projective linear group]]s {{math|PGL(2, ''q'')}} for {{math|1=''q'' =  5, 7, 9}}.<ref>[[Jean Dieudonné]] (1954) "Les Isomorphisms exceptionnals entre les groups classiques finis", [[Canadian Journal of Mathematics]] 6: 305 to 15 {{doi|10.4153/CJM-1954-029-0}}</ref>

If {{math|1=''q'' = 2{{sup|''n''}}}}, and given {{mvar|A}} and {{mvar|B}}, then the harmonic conjugate of {{mvar|C}} is itself.<ref>[[Emil Artin]] (1957) [https://archive.org/details/geometricalgebra033556mbp/page/n93/mode/2up?view=theater ''Geometric Algebra'', page 82] via [[Internet Archive]]</ref>

==Iterated projective harmonic conjugates and the golden ratio==
Let {{math|''P''{{sub|0}}, ''P''{{sub|1}}, ''P''{{sub|2}}}} be three different points on the real projective line. Consider the infinite sequence of points {{mvar|P{{sub|n}}}}, where {{mvar|P{{sub|n}}}} is the harmonic conjugate of {{math|''P''{{sub|''n''-3}}}} with respect to {{math|''P''{{sub|''n''-1}}, ''P''{{sub|''n''-2}}}} for {{math|''n'' > 2}}. This sequence is convergent.<ref>F. Leitenberger (2016) [http://forumgeom.fau.edu/FG2016volume16/FG201655index.html Iterated harmonic divisions and the golden ratio], [[Forum Geometricorum]] 16: 429–430</ref>

For a finite limit {{mvar|P}} we have 

:<math>\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{P_{n+1}P}{P_{n}P}=\Phi-2=-\Phi^{-2} = -\frac{3-\sqrt{5}}{2},</math>

where <math>\Phi=\tfrac{1}{2}(1+\sqrt{5})</math> is the [[golden ratio]], i.e. <math>P_{n+1}P\approx -\Phi^{-2} P_{n}P</math> for large {{mvar|n}}.
For an infinite limit we have

:<math>\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{P_{n+2}P_{n+1}}{P_{n+1}P_{n}}=-1-\Phi =-\Phi^{2}.</math>

For a proof consider the projective isomorphism 

:<math>f(z)=\frac{az+b}{cz+d}</math> 

with 

:<math>f \left ((-1)^n\Phi^{2n} \right )=P_n.</math>
